transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Leo Martinez (Redwood), Elena Ruiz (CISO), Tom Hargreaves, Priya Singh, Jason Cole

Summary:
Quick deep dive on Private/VPC security architecture for a potential Northbridge Private deployment. Focus on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, RBAC/SSO integration, audit logs and KMS/HSM encryption. Agreed to follow up with network diagrams, SOC2 docs, and sample rule sets.

Topics:
- Private control plane vs hosted control plane options
- VPC peering, transit, and egress controls (NAT/proxy)
- Firewalling: security groups, NACLs, FW appliances
- Bastion/jump hosts and IAM/RBAC mapping to SSO (Okta)
- Audit logging, SIEM integration, retention and evidence for SOC 2 / ISO 27001
- Encryption at rest (KMS/HSM) and in transit (mTLS)
- On-prem/air-gapped considerations and certificate rotation

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — we're going to walk through the Private VPC architecture and call out the typical ingress and egress patterns, firewalling, and how we integrate with customer KMS and SSO.
[00:32] Elena Ruiz (CISO): Great, thanks Samir. We are particularly interested in egress controls and auditability — for regs we need tight egress and long retention on logs.
[00:48] Maya Chen: Totally. Just to flag, there are two deployment patterns we usually propose: private control plane (customer-managed VPC with Redwood agents) or a private VPC with Redwood control plane but no public access, depending on compliance needs. Some customers call it Redbud Private in notes — it should be Redwood Private, sorry transcription confusions.
[01:15] Tom Hargreaves: Can you explain the difference in network flow? If we do private control plane, does anything go out to internet?
[01:30] Maya Chen: In the private control plane option, nothing leaves your VPC except the model weights fetch during onboarding if you choose hosted model sync — we can also pre-bundle models offline. For the standard private VPC with Redwood-managed control plane, we use VPC endpoints and strict egress via NAT or egress proxy; egress is limited to specific IPs and FQDNs and goes through your firewall.
[01:58] Priya Singh: How do you handle egress for telemetry and logs? We need to forward audit logs to our SIEM — Splunk in our case.
[02:10] Leo Martinez: We support pushing logs to customer-managed endpoints via secure TLS connections. For Splunk, we can forward over HTTPS to a Splunk HEC endpoint in your VPC or via a peered VPC. For high-security, customers prefer a direct VPC peering or private link to avoid public internet.
[02:36] Jason Cole: Any requirement for opening inbound ports? We're strict about ingress — inbound only via bastion or ALB with strict policies.
[02:45] Maya Chen: Inbound is only required if you need our control plane callbacks or debug access. For pure inference we support request-in - request-out via private endpoints. If you want the Redwood console, control plane can be placed in your VPC or accessible through a private link. Typically we recommend a bastion + SSH jump + session recording for SE debug sessions.
[03:12] Elena Ruiz: What about firewalling at subnet level — do you recommend security groups or full NGFW?
[03:20] Maya Chen: Security groups + NACLs are baseline. For deeper inspection we see customers put an NGFW (Palo Alto, Check Point) in the path for east-west traffic. We generally recommend segmentation: management/control subnets, inference subnets, and storage subnets. Control plane endpoints go in a management subnet with tight egress.
[03:45] Tom Hargreaves: How do you manage certs and mTLS? We require mutual TLS for service-to-service.
[03:53] Maya Chen: We support mTLS for all service-to-service traffic. Certs can be customer-managed — you can bring your own CA and we can rotate certs via an automated rotation process. On-prem air-gapped deployments can use an offline cert provisioning step.
[04:15] Priya Singh: Encryption at rest — do you integrate with customer KMS / HSM?
[04:21] Samir Patel: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS like AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and external HSMs via standard APIs. Keys can be customer-managed; we support envelope encryption. For the highest assurance we support FIPS-validated HSM integrations.
[04:38] Jason Cole: For audit logs, retention policy — we need logs for 7 years for certain data. Can you support extended retention?
[04:47] Leo Martinez: We ship logs to your storage backends — S3 with lifecycle policies or to a SIEM. We don't hold long-term logs in our control plane unless explicitly contracted. For Dedicated/Private, logs live in your storage and you control retention.
[05:12] Elena Ruiz: SOC 2 and ISO evidence: can you share your reports and scope?
[05:18] Samir Patel: Yes, we'll share SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certificates. We'll also include test reports and your requested scoping notes. I'll add that as an action item.
[05:30] Tom Hargreaves: Network flow example — if inference calls originate from our web tier in public subnets, what's the recommended path?
[05:40] Maya Chen: We recommend flow: public web tier -> internal API/gateway -> NAT/egress -> private inference endpoints in inference subnets. If you want private-only, you can put the web tier behind an internal ALB in a private subnet, or route through a proxy. Avoid having inference nodes in public subnets.
[06:05] Priya Singh: Any guidance on VPC peering vs Transit Gateway? We have a Transit GW setup for cross-account networking.
[06:12] Maya Chen: For larger orgs, Transit Gateway is cleaner; our deployment supports TGW attachments and we can advertise prefixes. For smaller setups VPC peering or PrivateLink is fine. The important part is ensuring security groups and route tables block unintended egress and east-west access.
[06:38] Jason Cole: Do you require opening port ranges for GPU nodes?
[06:43] Maya Chen: No open ranges; we show specific control plane ports. GPU nodes only need to talk to the local runtime and the management endpoint on a known port. We provide a reference firewall rule set in the checklist.
[07:00] Elena Ruiz: How do you handle RBAC when we have SSO in Okta? We need role mapping and SCIM provisioning.
[07:09] Samir Patel: We integrate with SAML SSO (Okta, Azure AD) and support SCIM for provisioning groups/users. RBAC maps to your IdP groups; we can sync groups and map to Redwood roles (admin, engineer, read-only). Audit logs capture role changes.
[07:34] Tom Hargreaves: Can authn/authz be enforced at network layer also?
[07:38] Maya Chen: Yes — we recommend defense in depth. Network policies plus service-level RBAC and mTLS ensures both network and application-level controls.
[07:50] Priya Singh: For pen tests and vulnerability scans — do you allow scanning of nodes and do you provide CVE patch timelines?
[07:58] Leo Martinez: We support customer-initiated scans in a scheduled window and provide patch timelines. For Private deployments we can coordinate maintenance windows and provide images with timely CVE fixes.
[08:20] Elena Ruiz: Data residency — we need processing and storage in EU only for some workloads. How do you partition?
[08:28] Samir Patel: We can pin workloads to regions and ensure models/data remain in the selected region. For Private deployments you control the region/VPC. We’ll include regional controls in the deployment playbook.
[08:45] Tom Hargreaves: Any quirks with KV cache — I sometimes see notes 'KV cash' in older docs — what is the caching surface that might store data?
[08:55] Maya Chen: The KV cache stores inference prefixes to speed up responses; in a Private deployment caches are ephemeral and live on the inference nodes; you control disk encryption and retention. We can flush caches on demand.
[09:12] Jason Cole: Can we enforce egress via a proxy so all outbound goes through a single auditing point?
[09:18] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Many customers route outbound through an egress proxy (Squid/Envoy) or NAT gateway with logging. We support proxy configuration and can send traffic over TLS to your proxy.
[09:34] Priya Singh: For SIEM integration, do you support structured audit logs (JSON) with field mapping?
[09:41] Leo Martinez: Yes — we provide structured JSON audit events with fields for user, action, timestamp, request id, model version. We can map fields to Splunk/ELK schemas.
[09:55] Samir Patel: Quick note on evidence: we can provide configuration snapshots, audit log samples, and test results as part of the compliance pack.
[10:05] Tom Hargreaves: On-prem/air-gapped — what's required?
[10:11] Maya Chen: For air-gapped, we do an offline install: container images and model bundles are provided via secure media or pre-loaded in your registry. Control plane can be managed by your team; we provide scripts for cert provisioning and KMS integration. There's more manual ops but it's supported.
[10:31] Elena Ruiz: How do you handle key rotation and proof of destruction?
[10:36] Leo Martinez: Keys are rotated via KMS policies; for BYOK/HSM we document rotation procedures. Proof of destruction is typically handled by KMS/HSM provider logs — we'll include the process in the runbook.
[10:52] Priya Singh: Are audit logs tamper-evident?
[10:56] Maya Chen: We recommend forwarding logs to an immutable store (S3 with Object Lock or WORM) or to a SIEM with append-only retention. We also support signing of audit records.
[11:10] Jason Cole: Can we get a sample architecture diagram and reference security group rules?
[11:15] Samir Patel: Yes — we'll send a reference diagram and a checklist (action item). Maya will draft firewall/security group examples.
[11:26] Tom Hargreaves: Any need for special IAM roles on our side?
[11:30] Maya Chen: We'll need a role for deployment automation and an optional cross-account role for S3 access if you want logs shipped. We'll include the exact IAM policy in the checklist.
[11:47] Priya Singh: What about vulnerability management for models and runtime?
[11:51] Leo Martinez: We scan runtime images and publish CVE bulletins; model-level vulnerabilities are rare but we have an eval process and model vetting.
[12:05] Elena Ruiz: Cost vs isolation tradeoffs — any quick notes?
[12:09] Samir Patel: More isolation (air-gapped, private control plane, dedicated infra) increases operational cost and lead time. We'll surface options in the pricing and pilot proposal.
[12:22] Tom Hargreaves: For the pilot, what telemetry will we get?
[12:26] Maya Chen: Token-level cost, latency, per-route metrics, and full request traces. We can also provide KV cache hit rates and GPU utilization.
[12:40] Priya Singh: Do you have an incident response playbook and runbooks for forensics?
[12:46] Leo Martinez: Yes — we provide an IR playbook, escalation contacts, and forensic artifacts (logs, snapshots) as part of enterprise onboarding.
[13:05] Jason Cole: Any blockers we should know before a pilot?
[13:09] Samir Patel: Mostly network approvals and an NDA for the pilot images if we need to share connectors. We'll coordinate with your security and legal teams.
[13:22] Elena Ruiz: Ok let's recap next steps.
[13:25] Samir Patel: Recap: we'll send SOC2/ISO paperwork, Private deployment checklist, sample firewall rules, and an architecture diagram. We'll schedule a network diagram deep dive with Tom/Jason on 2026-05-14. Pilot timeline TBD after NDA.
[13:45] Maya Chen: I'll prepare the sample rule set and NAT/egress config and include an example Transit Gateway attachment.
[13:54] Priya Singh: Thanks, that helps.
[14:00] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the checklist and docs.

End of transcript.
